reader.title: Lynching of Thomas J. Amos
bases: A mob seized Amos, a Black man accused of killing a white storekeeper, and hanged him from a tree (A2, A3, A5, A14).

Amos was hanged by a 'mob' or 'crowd' (the Washington Times says 'a mob of white men') with no lawful authority, after a reported confession to killing Jackson, i.e. as punishment for an alleged crime (A2, A3, A5, A14).
The Sun's Cheneyville dispatch, the Picayune special, a separate New Orleans dispatch and the local Colfax Chronicle agree that a mob hanged Amos after Jackson's killing (A2, A3, A5, A14).

summary.text: The lynching of Thomas J. Amos was the hanging of a Black man by a mob near Cheneyville, Louisiana, before daylight on August 29, 1900, hours after the shotgun killing of Alanson G. Jackson, a white storekeeper.
Accused of the killing, Amos was seized, was said to have confessed, and was hanged from a tree near the store where Jackson died.
Papers across the country featured his reported offer to climb the tree, jump, and "show you how a man can die."
Jackson had charge of Bennet's store at Bennettville, on Bayou Boeuf about five miles below Cheneyville.
According to the New York Sun, he and Amos had had "a difficulty" two weeks earlier, and Amos was said to have threatened him several times since.
The Lafayette Gazette called Jackson's killing the second "occurrence of that nature" near Cheneyville in a few days.
On the night of Tuesday, August 28, Jackson returned to the store from a dance at Cheneyville.

A special dispatch to the New Orleans Picayune said he was shot near the store's rear steps with both barrels of a gun loaded with buckshot, and that the gunman reloaded with bird-shot and fired again into the body.
Another New Orleans dispatch said his body was found "just in front of his house."
Accounts of the capture differ.
The Sun reported that a mob went to Amos's home, that he tried to fire on the approaching "squad," and that his aged father wrenched the gun away and turned him over.
The Picayune special said only that he stayed at his father's home, a mile from the store, "until arrested."
The Washington Times described his captors as "a mob of white men," the Colfax Chronicle as "a posse of men."
Taken back to the store and questioned, Amos was reported to have made a full confession, though the Washington Times said he "could give no reason for the murder."
At a nearby tree he was quoted as offering to put his own head in the noose and jump, and as inviting the crowd to shoot into his body.
The Washington Times and the Colfax Chronicle said the mob refused, hanged him, and riddled the body with bullets.
Within an hour the coroner was notified, and the Picayune special said the body was left hanging "as a warning to law-breakers."
No report of an inquest verdict, an arrest, or grand jury action appears in the coverage.
Jackson's brother-in-law, the Rev. A. L. Johnson, was called away from Baptist services at Colfax by telegram, and the Colfax Chronicle's account of the lynching followed.
The Bossier Banner noted a week later only that "Tom Amos, colored," had been lynched near Cheneyville.
White newspapers carried the story within a day in three versions: the Picayune special, a Cheneyville dispatch to the Sun, and a shorter New Orleans dispatch.
The Picayune special, which opened by calling the shooting "a most dastardly assassination," was reprinted in Savannah, Louisville, Houston, Bryan, Yorkville and, on September 3, Atlanta.

Short wire versions ran in the Washington Evening Star, the Indianapolis Journal, the Rock Island Argus and other papers, while the New Orleans dispatch, naming the dead man "Lawson Jackson," ran in the Washington Times and the Alexandria Gazette.

Headlines made Amos's conduct at the tree the story: "See How a Man Can Die" in the Sun, "Aided at His Own Lynching" in the Evening Star, and "Negro Lynched Himself. Queer Request" in the Atlanta Constitution.
Most versions called Amos "the murderer" or "the assassin" outright, treating the reported confession as settling his guilt, and the Courier-Journal's subhead called him "bloodthirsty."
Other headlines read "Mob Wreaked Its Vengeance" (Savannah), "This Was Not For Outrage" (Rock Island) and "Swift Retribution" (Colfax).
All coverage located was in white papers; no report was found in the Black press.
The dead man was "Alanson G. Jackson" in the Picayune special, the Sun and, in a garbled form, the Colfax Chronicle, but "Lawson Jackson" in the New Orleans dispatch and the Bossier Banner.
The Picayune special and the Sun said the body was left hanging and mention no shooting, while the Washington Times and the local Colfax Chronicle said it was riddled with bullets.

accounts.label: Sun's Cheneyville dispatch
accounts.gist: Prior quarrel and threats; mob went to Amos's home, his father disarmed him and handed him over; confession at the store; hanged, body left swinging.

accounts.label: Picayune special
accounts.gist: Detailed ambush at the store, Amos arrested at his father's home, full confession, hanged within an hour and left 'as a warning to law-breakers'.

accounts.label: New Orleans dispatch
accounts.gist: 'Tom Amos' arrested by 'a mob of white men' for killing 'Lawson Jackson' found in front of his house; confessed without giving a reason; mob refused his offer to hang himself and riddled the body.

accounts.label: Colfax Chronicle (local, via the dead man's brother-in-law)
accounts.gist: A 'posse of men' arrested the negro, who confessed with 'bravado', and hanged and riddled him.

framing.detail: The Picayune special calls the shooting 'a most dastardly assassination' and says the body was left 'as a warning to law-breakers'; Savannah headline 'Mob Wreaked Its Vengeance for a Bloody Assassination'.
The Sun headlines Amos's words, 'See How a Man Can Die', calling him 'A Negro Murderer'.
Short wires headed 'Aided at His Own Lynching', 'This Negro Wanted to Die', 'Lynchers' Victim Defiant', 'This Was Not For Outrage'.
Colfax Chronicle titles its account 'Swift Retribution'.
